title: The Science of Education, the Science of Learning and an Educational Establishment All at Sea
author: Vainker, Stephen
summary: Stephen Vainker draws a critical distinction between two projects: a 'science of education' -- the broad endeavor of determining what schools should prepare people for and how -- and the narrower 'science of learning,' which focuses on cognitive efficiency and retention. He argues that after the 1980s reduction of education to human capital maximization, the science of education became impossible, and the science of learning moved in to fill the space. Vainker uses Carl Hendrick as a case study: a prominent learning-science advocate who has recently consulted for Alpha school, whose every feature contradicts Hendrick's own published positions on whole books, knowledge, growth mindset, Duolingo, and screen time. The contradiction reveals something deep about the moment: those trained in the science of learning find themselves without a stable theory of what education is for, leaving them vulnerable to capture by well-resourced schools whose ideology fills the normative void. Vainker does not condemn Hendrick personally but uses the inconsistency to expose how the triumph of learning science over educational science leaves practitioners epistemically unmoored.
points: Vainker distinguishes the science of education (Bobbitt's 1918 vision: mapping what human life requires and designing curriculum accordingly) from the science of learning (optimizing cognitive efficiency), arguing they are not the same project.

The 1980s reduction of education to human capital maximization made a true science of education politically impossible, leaving learning science -- brain-based, efficiency-focused -- to dominate by default.

Carl Hendrick's contradiction in consulting for Alpha school, which violates his stated positions on books, knowledge acquisition, growth mindset, and screen time, illustrates what happens when learning science researchers lack a stable framework for educational purpose.

Without a normative theory of what education is for, practitioners trained in learning science have no principled basis to reject any school model that claims efficiency gains -- making them vulnerable to ideological capture.

The article implies that recovering a genuine science of education -- one that can say what schools are preparing students for and why -- is the unfinished business that learning science alone cannot complete.
quotes: This requires only that one go out into the world of affairs and discover the particulars of which these affairs consist. These will show the abilities, attitudes, habits, appreciations, and forms of knowledge that men need.

But in the 1980s the preparation for 'human life' was flattened into the preparation of 'human capital'; the purpose of education reduced to maximising the learning productivity of students to increase an abstracted sense of their economic value. But we do have a science of learning: a science that aims to increase the efficiency of learning through an understanding of how the brain learns.

Hendrick has raised eyebrows in working with AI-based private school chain Alpha, for the very simple reason that Alpha is at odds with almost all his stated educational beliefs: Hendrick has argued for the importance of whole books [ ]; Alpha uses Teach Tales, 'an AI-powered story-building platform that turns your kid into the author of their own custom adventures [ ]'. Hendrick has advocated for the importance of knowledge; Alpha [ ] emphasises engagement and extra-curricular activities, limiting academics to 2 hours and emphasising that all subjects (even history) are taught through hooking

His explanation [ ] for why he is working with Alpha is totally unconvincing: And then one thing that I saw really changed my mind which is this idea of of AI coaching. So what what they're working on now is a platform called timeback which will be where when you log on to the learning platform there's a sort of a monitoring element to it.

We know that from 20 years ago with the studies on MOOCs unless there's someone watching you unless there's someone kind of invested in you they're not going to do maybe the top 5% who are hugely motivated. So this platform will provide a what they're calling a waste meter.

In a fascinating segment [ ], he starts explaining that he doesn't want his daughters on screens, and then, trying to use this as a build up to a defence of Alpha, he... literally can't do it. He trails off and then explains the actual reason he is interested, which is that the AI-led learning environment can facilitate the development of the science of learning: So, we have lots of ethical questions about education.

And then the second thing is I want learning to be driven by the science of learning. I want it to be driven by what we know about human cognition about how we attend to process, retrieve, store information and knowledge, that change in long-term memory.
